This game was very positively reviewed. However, I found it to be very disappointing. The term 'game' might not apply, it was really just multi-media fiction with Simon Says style 'puzzles' "Simon didn't say cut the green wire!" The game scolds you for making a single mistake, literally your Supervisor in the game calls you and scolds you. The cut scenes are weird blurry messes with some background noise, but you can't skip, because it turns out there are clues in those that you need for later 'puzzles'. Thankfully they are about as subtle as a brick thrown through the window. I usually like these sorts of games, but this one was very disappointing.

This is a fun, albeit short, narrative puzzle game, the puzzles themselves are good, you're not left wondering how you were expected to solve them. The narrative is engaging, and if you pay attention you'll have worked out the ending before getting there. 
Other than dialogue variation and achievement hunting, you won't have any reason to replay the game other than to experience the story again, though this isn't a negative for a game like this as this genre of game tends to be a single shot deal.
I feel i should mention that the audio, environmental, voice acting, and soundtrack really are a highlight, it's not often you find an indie game like this with this much production value. The voice actors convey distinct characters, the ambient audio immerses you, and the music sets the tone of each scene very well.
With the recent announcement of a sequel I'm looking forward to what this team will do with the world they've built here.

Since I don't read about the games I buy, as I like the element of surprise without any ''spoilers'', I didn't know what to expect, but it wasn't this. I thought I'd just play my role as a federal analyst without a story and continuously work in the loop of solving cases (not that I would not enjoy that), but I was pleasantly surprised. Story addition was an excellent element, tho I would gladly welcome more cases, longer and more difficult. In my opinion, The Mole was also very obvious, and I was sad to discover I was right all along and completely stripped of the great revelation of their identity. Not to be all negative, the camera in Tanner's room and the identity of Sacha were very well thought out, and I appreciated it. Although there were things I'd change, as I already mentioned, I greatly enjoyed playing this game. You can get the idea what a job like this consists of (if we take into consideration only the investigation lol), and at the same time enjoy puzzles, detective work, let's say, mystery and a lot more. I recommend it for crime fanatics such as myself, because I believe we all dreamt of becoming a detective, an investigator, an analyst and similar jobs, but in general to people who enjoy some mystery.

Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

A cautions recommendation for fans of investigation games. The Operator feels like a distant successor to (the great) [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/368370/Her_Story/]Her Story[/url] with much less FMV and much more variety in gameplay. It's very well presented for a game composed mostly of interfaces and files, which supports immersion into the life of the protagonist. But it's also strictly linear, offering only the illusion of choice in dialogues and about zero replay value. Expect to complete it in 3 to 4 hours.

This was a very fun, albeit short, experience. It uses its limited gameplay devices to provide a compelling, bite-sized narrative. I honestly wish the game was a bit longer or had a spin-off that focused purely on the detective "operator" aspects. The way this story was told was unique without being too difficult. Honestly, the only janky part I could think of would be when it shows physical character models moving around, but it isn't that big of an issue. I'm not sure about the $14 price tag purely based on how long the game lasts, but it's an easy grab if it goes on sale or is in a bundle.

"Finally, a game where I can live my dream of working in a government office"

Sit at a desk. Click through files. Listen to awkward phone calls. Welcome to The Operator, where being nosy is not only allowed—it’s the whole job.

No jumpscares, no monsters, just you and a pile of cases that slowly get weirder (in a good way). Somehow, it makes digging through reports and audio logs actually fun. The twists are smart, the vibe is chill, and you’ll feel like a genius when you piece things together—until the game reminds you you're not.

If you’ve ever thought, “man, I wish I could be an overworked analyst with access to sensitive data,” this one’s for you.

This game would be perfect if it had more deduction/connection finding and more consequences for your actions (like branching narratives or multiple endings). The game play elements of finding clues and connecting them to other pieces of information was good, but there could've been 10x more to really fill out the game and make it feel more like you were really solving a mystery. It has the bones to be Roottrees meets Papers Please but it's just not there. And it's made worse by the fact that the story and mystery are actually really good. The mystery is compelling, the twist hit hard, the characters are likeable, the voice acting is great, but it just feels like a demo of what it could be.

Having that as a puzzle felt really cheap and lame.[/spoiler] That being said, my favorite part was [spoiler]defusing the bomb and I wish there had been more content like that.[/spoiler]

Story was mildly interesting but we have seen this hundreds of times before, [spoiler]mystical NWO organization controls the world behind the scenes, you can't trust your boss[/spoiler], yawn... the reveal at the end was at least interesting but that didn't really rescue the story for me.
